title: Three Ways Debt Kills a Developer: Spirals, Walls and Guarantee Calls
summary: Debt failures repeat in three patterns: leverage spirals that turn a fall in value into a fall in cash, maturity walls that ask for too much money on one date, and guarantee calls and cross-defaults that move a loss from one project to the person and to every other project. This lesson names each and the habits that contain it.
body:
Debt rarely kills a developer in one blow. It kills through three mechanisms: a leverage spiral that turns a fall in value into a fall in cash, a maturity wall that asks for too much money on one date, and a guarantee call that moves the loss from the project to the person. Learn to see all three.

Recall

Q. Why can an extension option fail exactly when you need it?

A. Because its conditions, such as a debt yield or coverage test, are usually set to the base case, and a missed notice window loses it. The test must be negotiated to the downside at signing.

Q. What does a tornado chart show?

A. The inputs of a model ranked by how far each one moves the result when changed by a set amount, so the widest bars, the ones to worry about first, sit at the top.

Q. Why does the order of a waterfall decide who wins?

A. Because cash is paid tier by tier: return of capital, the preferred return, any catch-up, then the split. Whoever sits earlier is paid first, and whoever sits later absorbs any shortfall.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Ford here, with Roman alongside for the lender's view. This week is the first of four post-mortems in the course. We do not study one failure; we study the patterns that repeat across many. In finance and debt, three patterns account for most of the wreckage. None of them needs fraud or incompetence. Each needs only leverage, time and a market that does not cooperate.

The leverage spiral

In plain English: when value falls, a heavily borrowed owner loses cash and control, which makes value fall further.

The professional framing is a leverage spiral: a feedback loop in which a fall in asset value breaches a loan-to-value or coverage covenant, which triggers a cash trap or sweep, which starves the property of the money needed for leasing and maintenance, which lowers income and value further. Equity is the first loss, so a modest fall in value is a large fall in equity.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A small portfolio is worth 100,000,000 dollars with 70,000,000 dollars of debt: loan to value of 70 percent and 30,000,000 dollars of equity. Values fall 15 percent, to 85,000,000 dollars. Debt is unchanged, so loan to value is now about 82 percent, and equity has fallen from 30,000,000 to 15,000,000 dollars: a 15 percent fall in value has halved the equity. Suppose the loans carry a maintenance covenant at 75 percent loan to value, a commercial term. It is breached. Cash is swept to the lender. The owner defers a roof and slows tenant improvements. Two tenants leave at lease expiry. Income falls, value falls again. The owner did nothing wrong after the first fall; the structure did it for him.

The maturity wall

In plain English: too much debt falling due in the same short period, when the market may be closed.

The professional framing is a maturity wall: a concentration of loan maturities in one period, which forces the borrower to refinance or sell a large amount at once, whatever the market conditions. A wall is harmless in an open credit market and lethal in a closed one, and you cannot choose which market you will meet.

A second worked example. Three buildings, each with a 20,000,000 dollar loan. Owner A has all three maturing in year 3. Owner B has them maturing in years 3, 5 and 7. In year 3 the lending market seizes. Owner A must find 60,000,000 dollars at once, or sell three buildings into a falling market. Owner B must find 20,000,000 dollars, can sell one building if necessary, and has two years before the next test. Same buildings, same income, same total debt. One owner survives the year and the other does not.

Say that out loud now.

A spiral turns lost value into lost cash; a wall asks for all the money on one date; a guarantee moves the loss to me.

The guarantee call and the chain between projects

In plain English: a guarantee is the moment a project's problem becomes your personal problem, and a cross-default is how one project's problem becomes every project's problem.

The professional framing has two parts. A guarantee call is the lender's written demand that the guarantor pay under a completion, cost-overrun, carry or repayment guarantee, or under a carve-out triggered by a defined bad act. A cross-default is a loan clause that makes a default under one loan, often including the borrower's or guarantor's other loans, a default under this one. Together they connect projects that you thought were separate. A developer with three projects in three special purpose vehicles may believe each stands alone. If he guaranteed all three, and each loan defaults when the guarantor defaults elsewhere, one bad building can put all three in default at once.

How the best do it

Well-run listed property companies commonly manage the same three risks with three habits. They spread debt maturities so that only a modest share of total debt falls due in any one year. They keep some properties free of mortgages and a committed bank facility undrawn, so they can repay a maturing loan without needing the market that day. And they set their own leverage limits well inside their lenders' covenants. A small developer can copy each one: no more than one major maturity a year; one unencumbered asset or a cash reserve equal to the largest single maturity; and a personal loan-to-value ceiling five to ten points below the covenant.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: a debt write-down, a foreclosure or a restructuring can create taxable income or a gain even when no cash changes hands; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: every guarantee and carve-out you sign is a path from the project to your own assets; list them. Banking: concentration with one lender deepens a relationship and also concentrates the risk of a single credit decision. Governance: require a board or partner approval before any new guarantee or cross-default is accepted. Estate: guarantees can survive death and bind the estate. Exit: a maturity wall can force an exit at the bottom of the cycle; ladder the dates.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on guarantee and cross-default terms; lender's counsel will be on the other side.

Why the three arrive together

Roman's note. A falling market lowers value, which starts the spiral. It closes credit, which turns the maturity schedule into a wall. And it raises defaults across the developer's projects at the same time, which calls the guarantees. Each mechanism makes the next one worse: a swept property cannot be sold well, a wall forces sales that lower comparable values, and a called guarantee drains the cash that might have defended another project. That is why the stress case must contain all three at once.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the three mechanisms arriving together, which they usually do because they share one cause, a falling market. The control is to test all three in one stress case: value down, credit closed for a year, and the largest guarantee called.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads each loan on its own and never draws the map of how his loans, guarantees and cross-defaults connect. Draw it once on one page: every loan, every maturity, every guarantee and every arrow between them.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick taught concentration on the personal balance sheet. Guarantees and cross-defaults are concentration you cannot see on the asset side: they put several projects onto one person. In Week 36, Priya taught that borrowing raises returns until it quietly lowers them. The spiral is the moment it turns.

Recap

Leverage spirals turn falling value into falling cash through covenants and sweeps. Maturity walls ask for too much money on one date. Guarantee calls and cross-defaults move losses from one project to the person and to every other project. Ladder maturities, hold an unencumbered reserve, set your own ceiling inside the covenant, and map every connection.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: General Growth Properties in 2009, a maturity wall at scale.
checklist: I have a one-page map of every loan, maturity, guarantee and cross-default.
No more than one major loan matures in any single year.
I hold an unencumbered asset or reserve equal to my largest single maturity.
My own loan-to-value ceiling sits five to ten points inside each covenant.
I know which loans default if I default elsewhere.
No new guarantee is signed without written approval.
I run one stress case with value down, credit closed for a year and my largest guarantee called.
head: Field checklist
speak: Debt kills a developer in three repeating ways. First, the leverage spiral: values fall, a loan-to-value covenant breaks, cash is swept, maintenance and leasing stop, and income and value fall again. On hypothetical numbers, a 15 percent fall in value on a 70 percent leveraged portfolio halves the equity. Second, the maturity wall: too many loans due in the same period, harmless in an open credit market and lethal in a closed one. Three 20,000,000 dollar loans due together need 60,000,000 at once; laddered, they need 20,000,000 a year. Third, the guarantee call and cross-default: the moment a project's loss becomes mine, and one project's default becomes every project's. So I ladder maturities, hold a reserve or an unencumbered asset equal to my largest maturity, set my own leverage ceiling inside the covenant, and map every connection on one page.
terms: Leverage spiral — a feedback loop in which falling value breaches covenants, cash is swept, the property is starved and value falls further.
Maturity wall — a concentration of loan maturities in one period that forces refinancing or sale whatever the market.
Cross-default — a clause making a default under another loan, of the borrower or guarantor, a default under this one.

hostile.q: You have three projects and you guaranteed all three. If one fails, what happens to the other two?
hostile.a: Today, two of the three loans cross-default to my guarantees, so a call on one could put the other two in default. I am renegotiating the cross-default in the next refinance to exclude non-recourse affiliate debt, I hold a cash reserve equal to my largest guarantee exposure, and the maturities are now in three different years, so no single date can force all three.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman on risk and the lender's view
title: General Growth Properties 2009: A Maturity Wall at Scale
summary: General Growth Properties filed for bankruptcy protection in April 2009 with malls that were still trading, because short-dated debt could not be refinanced once the credit markets closed. The seven steps show a mismatch between asset life and debt life, concentrated in time, and why good assets made the recovery possible.
body:
In April 2009, General Growth Properties, one of the largest shopping-mall owners in the United States, filed for bankruptcy protection. Its malls were still trading. Its tenants were still paying. What failed was its ability to refinance short-dated debt when the market for that debt closed.

Recall

Q. Name the three tests a permanent lender uses to size a refinance.

A. Loan to value, debt service coverage and debt yield. The smallest result is the loan, and the binding test can change when the market moves.

Q. What was the lesson of Dubai World in 2009?

A. The severe case arrives as a combination: prices, buyers and refinancing failed together because they shared one cause, so a plan built to survive each alone did not survive them together.

Q. In the Week 38 composite, what went wrong with the promote?

A. It was paid on interim gains before the investors had their capital and preferred return back, and when later losses arrived the clawback could not recover it, so the sponsor was effectively paid twice.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Ford here, with Roman. Most failures we study involve bad buildings, bad contracts or bad behaviour. This one is cleaner, which is why it teaches so much. The properties were productive. The problem was the shape of the debt. I keep to facts that were widely reported at the time and give no figures I cannot confirm; verify the details against the court record and the company's public filings before you rely on them. Where I describe how such a structure typically works, I describe the pattern, not any particular document.

1. Timeline

In 2004, General Growth Properties, based in Chicago, acquired the Rouse Company, another large mall owner, in a transaction financed heavily with debt. Through the mid-2000s, much of its borrowing was mortgage debt on individual malls, held in property-level companies, with relatively short maturities and an expectation that it would be refinanced, often through commercial mortgage-backed securities, loans pooled and sold to bond investors. In 2008, after the collapse of the credit markets, that refinancing market largely shut. The company faced large maturities in late 2008 and 2009 and sought extensions. Its share price collapsed. In April 2009 it filed for Chapter 11 protection in the United States, bringing in many of its property-level subsidiaries. It emerged from bankruptcy in November 2010, recapitalised with new equity from investors including Brookfield, and spun off a separate company, the Howard Hughes Corporation, holding its master-planned communities and some other assets.

2. Key decisions

Two decisions matter most. Financing a large acquisition largely with debt. And funding long-lived assets, malls expected to trade for decades, with debt that had to be refinanced every few years, much of it falling due in a narrow window.

3. Assumptions

The governing assumption was that refinancing would always be available for good properties at a price. For many years that was true. It was true because the market was open, not because the properties were good, and the two were treated as the same thing.

4. Incentives

Short-dated debt was usually cheaper than long-dated debt, so it raised reported earnings and returns in the good years. The cost of that choice, refinancing risk, did not appear in any annual figure until the year it was needed. The incentive structure paid for the saving every year and charged for the risk once.

5. Warning signs ignored

The concentration of maturities was visible in the company's own disclosures. The securitisation market slowed through 2007 before it shut in 2008. A maturity wall is the most forecastable risk in finance: the dates are written down years in advance. What cannot be forecast is the market on those dates, which is exactly why the dates must be spread.

Say that out loud now.

The dates are known years ahead; the market on those dates is not. So I spread the dates.

6. Point of no return

Roman's view is that, once the credit markets closed in 2008 with large maturities only months away, the remaining choices were all costly: sell assets into a falling market, raise equity at a punishing price, or seek court protection to restructure the debt. The time to act had been years earlier, when the maturities were being set.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a mismatch between the life of the assets and the life of the debt, concentrated in time. Operating performance was not the cause; it was the reason the outcome was eventually better than many feared.

Two lessons the lenders learned

First, the filing brought in property-level subsidiaries that many lenders had regarded as bankruptcy-remote special purpose entities, designed to stay outside a parent's bankruptcy. The court allowed those filings to proceed despite lender challenges. The lesson for a borrower and a lender alike: a ring-fence protects against some risks and not others, and its strength depends on law and facts at the time, not only on the documents. Second, because the malls kept earning, shareholders retained substantial value through the restructuring, which is unusual. A business with good assets and bad debt can be saved by fixing the debt; one with bad assets cannot.

The same mechanism, at small scale

A hypothetical developer owns four small apartment buildings, each worth 10,000,000 dollars with a 6,500,000 dollar loan, all four loans maturing in the same year to save a quarter point of margin. The year arrives with credit tight. Lenders will refinance at 55 percent of value, not 65. Each building needs 1,000,000 dollars of new equity, 4,000,000 in total, and the developer has 1,500,000. He sells one building at a discount to refinance the others. With maturities a year apart, he would have needed 1,000,000 in the first year and had time to see the market turn.

What a lender would check today

Roman's view from the other side of the table. After 2009, lenders to a sponsor with several properties routinely ask for a maturity schedule for the whole portfolio, not just the asset being financed. They ask what share of total debt falls due in each of the next five years, how much cash and undrawn committed facilities the sponsor holds, and how many properties are unencumbered. They ask whether any loan cross-defaults to sponsor debt. A developer who can hand over that page at the first meeting is treated as a better credit than one with a stronger building and no page. Prepare it before you are asked, update it quarterly, and you will find it changes the terms you are offered.

And they ask one more question, which you should ask yourself first: if no lender would refinance anything for twelve months, which loans fall due in that window, and where does the cash come from? If the answer is a sale, which property, at what discount, and what does that discount do to the covenants on the others?

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating cheap short debt as free money. The control is to price refinancing risk explicitly: for each maturity, the cash needed if lenders cut proceeds by ten points of loan to value, and a rule that no single year's need exceeds the reserve.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks good buildings protect him from a maturity wall. They protect the eventual recovery, not the date.

Callback

In Week 27, Ford studied Olympia and York, built on short money at the top of the cycle. General Growth Properties came more than fifteen years later, with different assets and a different market, and the same mismatch. That is what a post-mortem is for: recognising the mechanism when it reappears in different clothes.

The prevention rule

Rule 46: Never fund long-lived assets with debt that must be refinanced into a market I cannot control unless the maturities are laddered so no single year can force a sale, and I could survive a full year in which no lender will refinance.

Recap

General Growth Properties had productive malls and short, concentrated debt. When the refinancing market closed in 2008, the maturities became a wall and the company filed in April 2009, emerging in November 2010 after a recapitalisation. The root cause was asset life against debt life, concentrated in time.

Next: Roman, on The Money: what a called guarantee really costs, and why guarantees are called together.
checklist: I know the maturity date of every loan I am responsible for.
No single year's refinancing need exceeds my reserve.
I price refinancing risk as the cash needed if lenders cut proceeds by ten points of loan to value.
I do not accept a shorter term to save margin without pricing the refinance risk.
I know what my ring-fenced entities protect against and what they do not.
I could survive one full year with no refinancing available.
I reread my maturity schedule every quarter.
head: Field checklist
speak: In April 2009, General Growth Properties, one of the largest mall owners in the United States, filed for bankruptcy protection. Its malls were still trading and tenants were still paying. The problem was the shape of the debt. After a debt-financed acquisition of the Rouse Company in 2004, much of its borrowing was short-dated mortgage debt expected to be refinanced, often through securitisation. When that market closed in 2008, large maturities became a wall. The company restructured and emerged in November 2010 with new equity. The root cause was a mismatch between the life of the assets and the life of the debt, concentrated in time. The dates were known years ahead; the market on those dates was not. Rule 46: never fund long-lived assets with debt that must be refinanced into a market I cannot control unless the maturities are laddered and I could survive a full year with no refinancing at all.
terms: Commercial mortgage-backed securities — bonds backed by a pool of commercial property loans, sold to investors.
Bankruptcy-remote entity — a company designed, by its documents and structure, to stay out of its parent's insolvency.
Asset-liability mismatch — funding a long-lived asset with debt that falls due much sooner than the asset's useful life.

hostile.q: Your portfolio is good. Why do you need a reserve against refinancing at all?
hostile.a: Because a good portfolio protects the recovery, not the date. In 2008 good malls could not refinance because the market closed, not because the malls failed. My maturities are now laddered so only one major loan falls due in any year, and I hold a reserve equal to the cash that loan would need if lenders cut proceeds by ten points. If the market closes for a year, I wait; I do not sell.

rule: Rule 46: Never fund long-lived assets with debt that must be refinanced into a market I cannot control unless the maturities are laddered so no single year can force a sale, and I could survive a full year in which no lender will refinance.

title: What a Called Guarantee Costs, and Why They Are Called Together
summary: A guarantee costs its expected loss, but guarantees on projects in the same market are called together in the same bad year, so the honest number is the correlated one. This lesson prices both, shows how enforcement costs bring a guarantee into play early, and sets out the price of caps, burn-offs and reserves.
body:
A guarantee looks free at closing and costs nothing until it costs everything. Price it as an expected loss, then remember that guarantees are called together, in the same bad year, so the honest number is the correlated one.

Recall

Q. When a take-out appraisal comes in low, how should you split the gap?

A. Into the part time will fix, more income as the building stabilises, and the part it will not, the cap rate. Ask the lender only for what time can fix, and fund the rest.

Q. How do you size a reserve to the severe case?

A. Calculate the shortfall in the severe scenario over the period you must survive, then hold that amount as cash or committed funding, rather than sizing to the weighted or base case.

Q. What is a catch-up in a waterfall?

A. A tier after the preferred return in which the sponsor receives a large share of cash until its share of total profit reaches the agreed promote percentage.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman here. Yesterday Ford showed the wall. Today we price the moment the wall hits you personally. Lenders ask for guarantees because they reduce the lender's risk; that reduction has a value, and it is paid for out of your balance sheet. All figures are hypothetical round numbers.

The expected cost of one guarantee

In plain English: what you might pay, times how likely you are to pay it.

The professional framing is expected loss: the probability of a call times the amount you would pay, less what you could recover. A worked example. You guarantee 5,000,000 dollars of cost overrun on a project. You judge the chance of a call at 10 percent and the average call, if it comes, at 3,000,000 dollars. Expected loss is 300,000 dollars. That is the economic cost of the guarantee, and it belongs in your return on the project, even though it never appears in the pro forma.

Correlation: why guarantees are called together

In plain English: the bad year that calls one guarantee is the same bad year that calls the others.

The professional framing is correlation: the degree to which outcomes move together. Guarantees on different projects in the same market are highly correlated, because the same downturn widens cap rates, slows sales and closes credit for all of them at once.

A second worked example. You have guaranteed three projects, each with a possible call of 5,000,000 dollars and a 10 percent chance each. Treated as independent, expected loss is 1,500,000 dollars, and the chance of all three being called is one in a thousand. Treated honestly, in a downturn year the chance of a call on each rises to perhaps 60 percent and the calls arrive together. The relevant number is not the 1,500,000 dollar average but the 15,000,000 dollar combined call in the severe year. If your liquid assets are 4,000,000 dollars, the average says you are fine and the severe year says you are insolvent.

Say that out loud now.

Guarantees are called together, so I size to the combined call, not the average.

How leverage multiplies the call

The leverage spiral makes it worse. A guarantee of repayment on a 30,000,000 dollar loan, capped at 25 percent, is up to 7,500,000 dollars. At a 70 percent loan to value, the lender is covered by a 30 percent cushion of value. But an enforced sale is a forced sale: it costs fees, carry and a discount. If value falls 20 percent and enforcement costs a further 6 percent of value, the lender's recovery from a property once worth about 42,900,000 dollars is about 32,200,000 dollars, gross, and less once default interest and costs are added to the 30,000,000 dollar balance. The guarantee is suddenly in play, even though value fell less than the 30 percent cushion. Enforcement costs and default interest eat the cushion from both sides.

What the protections cost

Three protections reduce the correlated call, and each has a price. A cap on each guarantee, negotiated at signing, may cost a slightly higher margin or a lower loan. A burn-off, a clause that releases the guarantee once defined tests are met, such as completion or stabilised coverage, may need more equity or a longer period of reporting. A cash reserve sized to the severe combined call costs the return that cash would otherwise earn. On 15,000,000 dollars of exposure, holding even 5,000,000 dollars of reserve in cash rather than in a project might cost several hundred thousand dollars a year in foregone return. That is the honest price of sleeping at night.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. List every guarantee on a separate page, at the full amount you could be asked to pay, with the trigger, the cap and the burn-off date. Then add one line no bank form asks for: the combined call in a single bad year. Compare it with your liquid net worth. If the combined call exceeds your liquidity, you have not diversified across three projects; you have concentrated on one market through three documents. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of this for your own affairs.

Monthly thread: working with advisers

Ask your lawyer and your accountant the same question separately: what is my total exposure under every guarantee I have signed, in the worst single year? If their answers differ, you have found either a document one of them has not seen or an assumption you have not shared. Both are worth more than the fee.

Advisers answer the question you ask. Ask for the correlated number explicitly, and give them the full map of loans and guarantees, not one deal at a time.

A worked comparison: two developers, one bad year

Developer A has three projects, each with an uncapped 5,000,000 dollar guarantee, no burn-offs and 4,000,000 dollars of liquid assets. Developer B has the same three projects, each guarantee capped at 3,000,000 dollars, one already burned off at stabilised coverage, and 4,000,000 dollars of liquid assets plus a 2,000,000 dollar committed facility. The bad year arrives and all live guarantees are called.

Developer A faces 15,000,000 dollars of demands against 4,000,000 dollars of cash. He must sell what he can at a discount, and he cannot fund any defence of the projects, so the lenders' recoveries fall and the demands become final. Developer B faces 6,000,000 dollars against 6,000,000 dollars of available funds. He can pay, negotiate from strength, and keep his other assets. The difference in cost at signing was a slightly higher margin and a longer reporting period. The difference in the bad year was solvency.

One more test for your own numbers: ask which of your projects you would let go first if two guarantees were called in the same month. If you cannot answer in a sentence, you have not yet decided, and the decision will be made for you by whichever lender writes first.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is measuring guarantees one at a time and adding up averages. The control is a single severe-year number for all guarantees combined, compared with your liquid assets every quarter.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner signs a guarantee because the lender says everyone signs one. Everyone signs one; not everyone signs one uncapped, with no burn-off, on top of two others in the same market.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught that the severe case is a combination with a shared cause. Guarantees are the personal version of that lesson: the cause that calls one calls all, so they must be stressed together.

Recap

Price a guarantee as expected loss, then size your protection to the correlated severe-year call, because guarantees are called together. Enforcement costs and default interest eat the lender's cushion and bring guarantees into play sooner than value alone suggests. Caps, burn-offs and reserves cost something; compare that price with the combined call, not the average.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: cross-default, acceleration and how a guarantee is called.
checklist: I record every guarantee at its full possible call, with trigger, cap and burn-off.
I calculate the expected loss of each guarantee and include it in the project's return.
I calculate the combined call on all guarantees in one severe year.
I compare the combined call with my liquid net worth every quarter.
I negotiate a cap and a burn-off on every guarantee.
I allow for enforcement costs and default interest when judging the lender's cushion.
I give my advisers the full map, not one deal at a time.
head: Field checklist
speak: A guarantee costs its expected loss: the chance of a call times what I would pay. On a hypothetical 5,000,000 dollar overrun guarantee with a 10 percent chance and an average call of 3,000,000, that is 300,000 dollars, and it belongs in my return. But guarantees on projects in the same market are correlated: the downturn that calls one calls the others. Three guarantees of 5,000,000 each average 1,500,000 of expected loss, yet in the severe year all three can be called together, 15,000,000 at once. If my liquidity is 4,000,000, the average says I am fine and the severe year says I am insolvent. Enforcement costs and default interest also eat the lender's cushion, so guarantees come into play sooner than value alone suggests. So I negotiate caps and burn-offs, hold a reserve, and size to the combined call, not the average.
terms: Expected loss — the probability of a loss multiplied by its size, less recoveries.
Correlation — the degree to which outcomes move together, so that one bad event raises the chance of others.
Burn-off — a clause releasing a guarantee once defined tests, such as completion or stabilised coverage, are met.

hostile.q: You have guaranteed three projects. What is your exposure if all three are called in the same year?
hostile.a: Up to 15,000,000 dollars before caps, and 9,000,000 after the caps we negotiated. Two of the three burn off at stabilised coverage, which one has already met, so today's severe-year number is 6,000,000 dollars. I hold 5,000,000 in cash and a committed facility for the rest, and I report that combined number to you every quarter.

title: Cross-Default, Acceleration and How a Guarantee Is Called
summary: A guarantee call rests on a chain of clauses: events of default, acceleration, cross-default or cross-acceleration, and the guarantee's own terms. This lesson reads each link, shows how a small dispute on one project can reach a performing loan on another, and lists what to negotiate at signing.
body:
A guarantee is called by a letter, but the right to send it is built from a chain of clauses: default, acceleration, cross-default and the guarantee's own terms. Read the chain before you sign it, because by the time the letter arrives, the chain is complete.

Recall

Q. What is on an exit card?

A. The maturity date, the realistic stabilisation date, the take-out sized by three tests at today's and stressed numbers, the refinance gap and its funded source.

Q. What is the ladder of consequences in a loan?

A. A cash trap holds distributions, a cash sweep applies trapped cash to the loan, and an event of default lets the lender accelerate and enforce.

Q. Why does the tax character of a developer fee matter?

A. Because the same dollar may be taxed differently as a fee, a share of profit or a return of capital, so the label in the documents changes the after-tax result.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, LEX here. On Day 3 Roman priced a guarantee call. Today we read how a lender legally gets there, so that you can see where in the chain you still have choices. This is conceptual; the enforceability of every clause depends on the governing law and the document. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Events of default and acceleration

In plain English: a default gives the lender rights, and acceleration is the right to demand the whole loan now.

The professional framing is acceleration: the lender's right, after an event of default, to declare the whole outstanding loan immediately due, rather than waiting for scheduled payments. Some loans accelerate automatically on certain events, such as insolvency; most require the lender to give notice. Some defaults carry a grace period, a set time after the event before it becomes a default, or a cure period, a set time to fix it. These periods are commercial terms negotiated in the document.

Cross-default and cross-acceleration

In plain English: cross-default lets a problem on another loan count as a problem on this one.

The professional framing distinguishes two clauses. Cross-default treats a default under another specified debt, often of the borrower, its affiliates or the guarantor, as a default here, whether or not that other lender has acted. Cross-acceleration is narrower: it applies only once the other debt has actually been accelerated. The difference matters. Under cross-default, a minor covenant breach on another loan, one that lender may be willing to waive, can let this lender act first. Under cross-acceleration, nothing happens here unless the other lender takes the serious step. Borrowers usually seek cross-acceleration, a minimum threshold so that small debts do not trigger it, and an exclusion for non-recourse debt of separate affiliates.

A worked example, hypothetical. You have three project loans. Loan A contains cross-default to any debt of the guarantor over 100,000 dollars. A supplier dispute on Project C leads to a 150,000 dollar judgment against you as guarantor, unpaid while you contest it. Under Loan A's clause, that may be an event of default on Project A, a performing building, letting Lender A accelerate a 20,000,000 dollar loan over a 150,000 dollar dispute. Under cross-acceleration with a 1,000,000 dollar threshold, nothing happens.

Say that out loud now.

Cross-default counts their default; cross-acceleration waits for their action. I ask for cross-acceleration with a threshold.

How a guarantee is called

The guarantee is a separate contract between the lender and the guarantor. Read four things in it.

First, is it a guarantee of payment or of collection? Under a guarantee of payment, the lender can usually demand from you as soon as the borrower fails, without first pursuing the borrower or the property. Under a guarantee of collection, it must usually exhaust its remedies first. Most lenders insist on payment.

Second, the waivers. Guarantees typically contain long lists of waived defences: that the lender changed the loan, extended time, released security or failed to enforce first. In many jurisdictions, a guarantor may be discharged if the main contract is materially changed without consent, and the waivers exist to remove that protection. Read them, because they decide whether an extension you never approved still binds you.

Third, the demand mechanics: written notice to a stated address, a period to pay, and what the demand must state.

Fourth, the cap and the burn-off, the two clauses Roman priced yesterday, and whether either is lost on a default.

Standstill and the order of enforcement

When several lenders and guarantees are involved, the order in which they act decides who recovers. A standstill agreement, a contract among creditors and the borrower not to enforce for a period, is often the first step in a workout, giving time for a plan. Intercreditor agreements, from Week 37, may already restrict what junior lenders may do. A second example, hypothetical: a senior lender and a mezzanine lender, each with a guarantee from you. The intercreditor bars the mezzanine lender from enforcing its pledge for 90 days after a senior default, but says nothing about its guarantee. The mezzanine lender cannot touch the building, and can still call you. Read every guarantee against the intercreditor, not on its own.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, licensed in the governing law of each loan and guarantee.

What to negotiate at signing

Cross-acceleration rather than cross-default; a materiality threshold; an exclusion for non-recourse affiliate debt; grace and cure periods for non-monetary defaults; a cap and a burn-off on every guarantee; notice to the guarantor of any borrower default; and a consent right, or at least notice, before material changes to the loan. Each costs the lender a little control. Each can decide whether a dispute on one project becomes a crisis on three.

Reading a demand letter

When the letter arrives, read it against the guarantee before you answer it. Does it go to the address and in the form the guarantee requires? Does it state the default relied on? Does the amount demanded stay inside the cap, and does it include items, such as default interest or costs, that the guarantee does or does not cover? Was any condition, such as prior notice to the guarantor of the borrower's default, met? A defective demand is rarely fatal to the lender, because it can usually send another, but each defect is a fact your lawyer can use, and some guarantees make timing or form a condition of liability. Never ignore the letter, and never answer it yourself. Send it to counsel the same day, with the guarantee, the loan agreement, the intercreditor and your record of every notice you received.

Then diarise the response period, because silence can be treated as refusal and can bring forward the lender's next step.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a cross-default clause you never noticed that links a performing project to a troubled one. The control is a cross-default map: for each loan, which other debts can trigger it and at what threshold.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes a guarantee can only be called after the building is sold and a shortfall is proven. Under a guarantee of payment, the demand can come the day after default.

Callback

In Week 40, LEX read guarantees and carve-outs: loss carve-outs and springing recourse. Today adds the chain that reaches them. A carve-out is the trigger; acceleration and cross-default are how one trigger pulls on every loan you have.

Recap

Default gives rights; acceleration makes the whole loan due. Cross-default counts another lender's default, cross-acceleration waits for its action, so ask for the second, with a threshold and an exclusion for separate non-recourse debt. Read every guarantee for payment or collection, waivers, demand mechanics, cap and burn-off, and against the intercreditor.

Next: Roman, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a called guarantee.
checklist: I have a cross-default map for every loan, with thresholds.
I ask for cross-acceleration rather than cross-default, with a materiality threshold.
Non-recourse debt of separate affiliates is excluded from cross-default.
I know whether each guarantee is of payment or of collection.
I have read the waivers in every guarantee.
Every guarantee has a cap, a burn-off and a notice requirement.
I read each guarantee against the intercreditor agreement.
head: Field checklist
speak: A guarantee is called by a letter, but the right to send it is a chain. An event of default gives the lender rights. Acceleration makes the whole loan due now. Cross-default lets a default on another debt, of the borrower, an affiliate or the guarantor, count as a default here, even if the other lender has done nothing. Cross-acceleration waits until the other lender actually accelerates, so I ask for that, with a materiality threshold and an exclusion for separate non-recourse debt. In the guarantee itself I read four things: whether it is a guarantee of payment, which can be called at once, or of collection; the waivers of my defences; the demand mechanics; and the cap and burn-off. And I read every guarantee against the intercreditor agreement, because a lender barred from the building may still call me. Every point needs a lawyer licensed in the governing law.
terms: Acceleration — a lender's right, after default, to declare the whole loan immediately due.
Cross-acceleration — a clause triggered only when another debt has actually been accelerated, narrower than cross-default.
Guarantee of payment — a guarantee the lender can call as soon as the borrower fails, without first pursuing the borrower or the security.

hostile.q: Why should I accept cross-acceleration instead of cross-default? I want to act early.
hostile.a: You will still act early on this loan: every covenant and payment default here is yours to enforce at once. What cross-default adds is the right to accelerate a performing loan because of a small dispute elsewhere that its own lender might waive. A 1,000,000 dollar threshold and cross-acceleration protect you from my serious failures and protect both of us from a forced crisis over a minor one.

title: Reverse Engineering a Called Guarantee
summary: Starting from a 6,000,000 dollar guarantee demand, this lesson works back through the lender's claim, the forced-sale proceeds and the implied cap rate to split the damage between market, income and enforcement. Half the demand came from the costs of default itself, which shows why the guarantor must act before default.
body:
Start from the letter: a demand for 6,000,000 dollars under your guarantee. Work backward through the sale, the costs and the cap rate, and you find how far the market moved, how much of the loss was enforcement itself, and what would have stopped the letter being written.

Recall

Q. What is a leverage spiral?

A. A feedback loop in which falling value breaches a covenant, cash is swept, the property is starved of leasing and maintenance money, and income and value fall again.

Q. Why does a fall in rent cut NOI by a larger percentage?

A. Because operating expenses are largely fixed, so they do not fall with rent, and the whole fall lands on NOI.

Q. How do you reverse engineer a waterfall?

A. Start from what each party was paid, then work back tier by tier to the profit and hurdles that must have produced it, revealing the assumptions in the deal.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman here. Even weeks we work backward. Today the finished outcome is the worst one: a guarantee called. Reverse engineering a failure tells you which variable did the damage and how much room you really had. All figures are hypothetical round numbers; lending terms are commercial practice used for illustration.

The outcome

A lender sends a demand to the guarantor for 6,000,000 dollars under a repayment guarantee capped at 25 percent of the original loan. The loan was 30,000,000 dollars on a stabilised building with net operating income (NOI) of 2,100,000 dollars, valued at 5 percent cap rate at origination, so 42,000,000 dollars, about 71 percent loan to value. The lender has sold the building through enforcement. We want to know what happened.

Step 1: the lender's claim

At the date of sale, the lender's claim is the principal of 30,000,000 dollars plus accrued interest, default interest and enforcement costs. Suppose the lender's statement shows 1,500,000 dollars of default and accrued interest and legal and receiver costs. The claim is 31,500,000 dollars.

Step 2: the net proceeds

The shortfall demanded is 6,000,000 dollars, within the 7,500,000 dollar cap, so it is the full shortfall. Net proceeds must therefore have been 31,500,000 less 6,000,000, which is 25,500,000 dollars.

Step 3: the gross sale price

A forced sale carries brokerage, transfer costs and a receiver's fees on the sale. Suppose these were 1,500,000 dollars. The gross price was 25,500,000 plus 1,500,000, which is 27,000,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Claim, less demand, gives net proceeds; net proceeds plus sale costs give the price.

Step 4: the implied cap rate

Suppose NOI at the time of sale had fallen to 1,890,000 dollars, 10 percent below origination, because swept cash had delayed leasing. The buyer's cap rate was 1,890,000 divided by 27,000,000, which is 7 percent. So two things moved: income down 10 percent and the cap rate up two full points, from 5 to 7 percent.

Step 5: splitting the damage

Separate the causes. At the original NOI of 2,100,000 and 7 percent, value would have been 30,000,000 dollars, so the cap rate alone cost 12,000,000 dollars of value. The 10 percent income fall at 7 percent cost a further 3,000,000 dollars. Enforcement added the 1,500,000 dollar default and costs claim and the 1,500,000 dollar sale costs. In total, value fell 15,000,000 dollars, from 42,000,000 to 27,000,000, of which 80 percent was the cap rate. And 3,000,000 dollars of the 6,000,000 dollar demand, half of it, came from the costs of default and enforcement themselves.

Step 6: the table

ItemDollars
Value at origination, NOI 2,100,000 at 5 percent42,000,000
Loss from cap rate, 5 to 7 percentminus 12,000,000
Loss from NOI falling 10 percentminus 3,000,000
Gross sale price27,000,000
Sale costsminus 1,500,000
Net proceeds25,500,000
Lender's claim, principal plus interest and costs31,500,000
Guarantee demand6,000,000

Step 7: the break-even

What price would have avoided any call? Net proceeds must cover the claim, 31,500,000 dollars, so the gross price needed was 33,000,000 dollars. At the reduced NOI of 1,890,000, that is a cap rate of about 5.73 percent. The building could absorb a move of only about three quarters of a point before the guarantee was in play, despite a 29 percent equity cushion at origination. The cushion was real; it was simply eaten by income loss and the costs of failure.

Step 8: what would have stopped the letter

Three earlier actions change the answer. A paydown or a refinance before default would have avoided the 3,000,000 dollars of default interest, receiver and forced-sale costs; at that point the shortfall falls to about 3,000,000 dollars. A reserve that kept leasing funded during the sweep would have held NOI at 2,100,000, worth 3,000,000 dollars at 7 percent. Together those two leave a gap of zero. And a negotiated cap at 15 percent rather than 25 would have limited the demand to 4,500,000 dollars even with everything else unchanged.

Step 9: check forward

NOI 1,890,000 divided by 0.07 is 27,000,000. Less 1,500,000 costs, 25,500,000. Claim 31,500,000 less 25,500,000 is 6,000,000, inside the 7,500,000 cap. The numbers close.

Step 10: the same building with a lower loan

Run the same failure with one change at origination: a 26,000,000 dollar loan instead of 30,000,000, about 62 percent loan to value, with the extra 4,000,000 dollars as equity. At sale, with the same income fall and cap rate move, the gross price is still 27,000,000 dollars and net proceeds are 25,500,000. The claim, with interest and costs scaled down roughly in proportion, is about 27,300,000. The shortfall is about 1,800,000 dollars instead of 6,000,000. Four million dollars of equity at the start removed more than four million dollars of personal exposure at the end, because it reduced both the principal and the default costs that ride on it.

Step 11: what each variable is worth

Turn the table into a simple guide. Each quarter point of cap rate on this building is worth about 1,000,000 dollars of value near a 7 percent cap rate, and about 2,000,000 near 5 percent, because the same move matters more when rates are low. Each 1 percent of NOI is worth about 270,000 dollars at a 7 percent cap rate. Each month of default before the sale adds interest and costs, in this example on the order of a hundred thousand dollars or more. The cap rate is the variable you cannot control, the income is the one you can defend, and the months in default are the one you can stop. Spend your effort on the second and third.

The practical habit is to run this backward calculation on your own buildings before anything goes wrong: start from a hypothetical demand and find the price, cap rate and income that would produce it. If the cap rate that triggers the guarantee is within a point of today's market, the guarantee is not remote; it is one bad year away.

A last point on method. Every number in this example came from the lender's statement, the sale contract and the rent roll, all documents you will have. Ask for the lender's claim breakdown in writing as soon as a default looms, so that you are reconstructing the shortfall from its own figures rather than guessing at them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is believing the equity cushion at origination protects the guarantor. Enforcement costs, default interest and starved income consume it. The control is to model the guarantee against a forced sale, with costs, not against a calm valuation.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner waits for the sale to see the shortfall. Half the demand in this example was the cost of waiting.

Callback

In Week 10, Roman showed that a cap rate move hits equity first. Here it went further: through the equity and into the guarantor. The same one-line formula, value equals income over rate, drove the whole letter.

Recap

Work back from the demand: claim, net proceeds, gross price, implied cap rate. Split the damage between cap rate, income and enforcement. Find the break-even price. Act before default, because default interest and forced-sale costs are often half the call.

Next: Roman, on The Room: the meeting after the demand letter arrives.
checklist: I can work back from a demand to net proceeds, gross price and implied cap rate.
I separate the loss into cap rate, income and enforcement costs.
I model guarantees against a forced sale with costs, not a calm valuation.
I know the break-even sale price at which no guarantee is called.
I fund leasing and maintenance through any cash sweep.
I act before default, while default interest and receiver costs can still be avoided.
I check every backward answer forward.
head: Field checklist
speak: Start from a hypothetical 6,000,000 dollar demand under a guarantee capped at 25 percent of a 30,000,000 dollar loan. The lender's claim was principal plus 1,500,000 of default interest and costs: 31,500,000. Less the demand gives net proceeds of 25,500,000. Add 1,500,000 of sale costs: a gross price of 27,000,000. With income down 10 percent to 1,890,000, the buyer's cap rate was 7 percent, against 5 at origination. Split the damage: the cap rate cost 12,000,000 of value, the income fall 3,000,000, and enforcement 3,000,000, half the demand. The break-even cap rate was only about 5.73 percent, despite a 29 percent equity cushion at the start. So I model guarantees against a forced sale with costs, I keep leasing funded through any sweep, and I act before default, because the cost of failing is often half the call.
terms: Net proceeds — the sale price less the costs of selling, which is what the lender actually recovers.
Receiver — a person appointed, by a court or under the security documents, to take control of a property and manage or sell it for the lender.
Shortfall — the amount by which a lender's claim exceeds what it recovers from the security.

hostile.q: Your demand letter is for 6,000,000 dollars. Why should we negotiate rather than enforce against you?
hostile.a: Because half of that number is cost, and both of us lose it if we fight. If we settle now, the receiver and litigation costs stop. I can pay 2,000,000 dollars within thirty days and 1,500,000 over twelve months, secured on a property I own outright. That gives you a certain 3,500,000 dollars now, against a contested claim, against an asset you would have to locate, at a cost you would bear first.

title: The Meeting After the Demand Letter Arrives
summary: After a lender sells a building and demands payment under your guarantee, the meeting is about replacing a contested claim with a certain settlement. This lesson gives the lines to say and never to say, when to stay silent, how to hold your state and two contrasting outcomes.
body:
When a lender's demand letter arrives, the guarantor's meeting is about one thing: replacing a contested claim with a certain settlement. Arrive with facts, a number and a reason the lender is better off taking it.

Recall

Q. What did General Growth Properties teach about maturities?

A. The dates are known years ahead but the market on those dates is not, so maturities must be laddered and the owner must survive a year with no refinancing.

Q. How do you present a downside to a committee that wants the deal?

A. State the nearest threshold, then the combination that reaches it, then priced actions with their annual cost, and stop talking after the cost.

Q. How should you walk a partner through your waterfall?

A. Tier by tier with one set of numbers, showing who is paid what at each level and where the partner's money sits, before any discussion of the promote.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman here. Most guarantee calls end in a negotiation, not a judgment. The meeting after the letter decides whether that negotiation costs a fraction of the demand or the whole of it plus fees. All figures are hypothetical.

The scene

The lender has enforced on a building, sold it and sent a demand for 6,000,000 dollars under your repayment guarantee. Your lawyer has asked for a meeting with the lender's workout officer, the person in a bank responsible for loans in default, and its counsel. You arrive with your lawyer. The workout officer opens: "The guarantee is unconditional. We expect payment in thirty days."

The question behind the question

The surface statement is a demand. The real questions are three. How much can this guarantor actually pay? How long and how costly would it be to collect by force? And is there anything in the documents or the enforcement that weakens our claim? The workout officer is paid to recover the most, net of cost and time. Your job is to show that a settlement now is that number.

The lines to say

Acknowledge without conceding. "We have your demand and we take it seriously. We are here to resolve it, not to delay it."

Then the facts that matter to the lender, with your lawyer's agreement in advance on what you disclose. "Here is a sworn statement of my liquid assets and my other guarantees. You will see that my liquidity is about 4,000,000 dollars, and that two other lenders hold guarantees as well."

Then the questions about the claim, raised by counsel rather than by you. "We have questions about the default interest and receiver costs in the claim, about 3,000,000 dollars of it, and about whether the sale process obtained full value."

Then the proposal. "We propose 2,000,000 dollars within thirty days and 1,500,000 over twelve months, secured on a property I own without a mortgage, in full settlement and release."

Say that out loud now.

We take it seriously, here is what I can pay, here is what is uncertain in your claim, here is a certain number now.

The lines never to say

Never say "I don't have the money" without the statement to prove it; it invites investigation. Never say "your appraiser sold it too cheap" yourself; let counsel raise the sale process in writing. Never threaten bankruptcy as a tactic; if it is real, your counsel will say it in the right words at the right time. Never move assets after the demand; transfers to avoid creditors can be reversed and can create new liability, which Omar and Tessa cover later in the course. And never agree to anything in the room without your lawyer's review.

When to stay silent

After the proposal, stop. The workout officer must compare your certain 3,500,000 dollars with an uncertain larger number. That comparison happens in silence or in a call to credit, not in your explanation. If you fill the silence, you will offer more before you know the lender needs it.

Holding your state

A personal demand feels like an attack on your family's security, and that feeling pushes you either to plead or to fight. Neither works. Before the meeting, rehearse your four lines aloud with your lawyer playing the officer. In the room, sit back, speak slowly and refer to the statement on the table rather than to your feelings. Kema's practice from Week 4: slow breathing before you go in, in the car park, with the engine off.

Worked examples: two outcomes

Outcome one. The guarantor argues that the lender wrecked the sale, refuses to disclose assets and leaves. The lender sues. Two years later, after legal fees on both sides, judgment is given for 6,000,000 dollars plus interest and costs. The guarantor's other lenders, seeing the judgment, call their own guarantees under cross-default. The cost has grown, and it has spread.

Outcome two. The guarantor discloses, counsel raises the cost questions in writing, and a proposal of 3,500,000 dollars secured on a clean property is on the table. The lender counters at 4,200,000. They settle at 3,900,000, with a full release and no admission. The guarantor's other lenders are notified that the matter is resolved, which counsel had checked would not trigger their clauses. Painful, finished, contained.

After the meeting

Your lawyer confirms the discussion in writing, marked as without prejudice if your jurisdiction recognises that protection; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. You update your map of guarantees and your combined severe-year number. You write a decision journal entry: what you expected, what happened and what you would negotiate differently in the next guarantee.

What the workout officer is weighing

Your proposal is judged on three numbers. The present value of what you offer, which is high if it is paid quickly and secured. The expected value of suing you: the full claim times the chance of winning and collecting, less legal costs and two or more years of delay. And the effect on the lender's own reporting: a settled, closed file is worth something to a bank that must report losses. A sworn liquidity statement lowers the second number, because it shows how little there is to collect. Security on a clean property raises the first. Counsel's questions about default interest lower the claim itself. Together they move the lender from "full amount" to "best certain amount", which is the only negotiation that ends well for both sides.

If the lender refuses

If the lender will not engage, do not escalate in the room. Ask for its position in writing, take it to counsel, and consider whether a mediator, a neutral third party who helps the two sides reach a settlement, would help. Many workouts that fail in the first meeting settle within a few months once the costs of litigation become visible to both sides.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting emotion choose fight or surrender. The control is preparation: a sworn liquidity statement, a cost analysis of the claim, an agreed proposal and walk-away number, all settled with counsel before the meeting.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner goes to the meeting alone, to keep it friendly. A guarantor without counsel will say something in the first five minutes that costs more than the fee.

Callback

In Week 7, Roman ran the guarantee meeting at the start: the lender asking what you are worth. This is the same meeting at the end. Everything you disclosed then, and every guarantee you signed since, is on the table now. A balance sheet kept honestly from the start is the strongest thing you can bring to this room.

Recap

Acknowledge the demand, disclose what you can pay, let counsel question the claim, propose a certain settlement, then stay silent. Never plead, threaten or move assets. Settle with a release, contain the effect on other lenders and update your map.

Next: Kema, with the week's review: six questions, the Red Pen and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I never attend a guarantee meeting without my lawyer.
I bring a sworn statement of liquid assets and other guarantees, agreed with counsel.
Counsel has analysed default interest, costs and the sale process in the claim.
I have an agreed proposal and walk-away number before I go in.
I stay silent after making the proposal.
I never move assets after a demand.
Any settlement includes a full release, and counsel checks its effect on other lenders.
I update my guarantee map and decision journal afterwards.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a demand letter arrives under my guarantee, the meeting has one purpose: to replace a contested claim with a certain settlement. I go with my lawyer. I acknowledge the demand without conceding it. I disclose, with counsel's agreement, a sworn statement of my liquidity and my other guarantees, because the lender wants to know what I can actually pay. Counsel, not I, raises the uncertain parts of the claim, such as default interest, receiver costs and the sale process. Then I make a proposal: a certain sum now, secured on a clean asset, in full settlement and release. Then I stop talking. I never plead, never threaten bankruptcy as a tactic, never blame the appraiser myself and never move assets after a demand. Afterwards counsel confirms in writing, I check the settlement will not trigger other lenders' clauses, and I update my guarantee map.
terms: Workout officer — the lender's specialist responsible for loans in default and for recovering the most, net of cost and time.
Release — a written agreement by which a creditor gives up further claims in exchange for a settlement.
Without prejudice — a protection, recognised in some legal systems, that keeps settlement offers out of evidence if negotiations fail.

hostile.q: Your guarantee is unconditional. Why would we take less than 6,000,000 dollars?
hostile.a: Because collecting 6,000,000 is not certain, and it is not free. About 3,000,000 of the claim is default interest and enforcement cost that we will contest, my liquid assets are about 4,000,000, and two other lenders hold guarantees too. I am offering 3,500,000 dollars, 2,000,000 within thirty days and the rest secured on an unmortgaged property. That is certain money now against an expensive claim later.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 46 Review: Leverage Spirals, Maturity Walls and Guarantee Calls
summary: Six questions with answers on leverage spirals, maturity walls, General Growth Properties, cross-default, the arithmetic of a called guarantee and the meeting after a demand letter. A recap, a Red Pen drill on a misleading debt summary, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: debt kills through spirals, walls and guarantee calls, and all three share one cause, so ladder the dates, size to the combined call and act before default.

Recall

Q. Why are guarantees called together?

A. Because guarantees on projects in the same market are correlated: the downturn that calls one raises the chance of calls on the others, so the honest number is the combined severe-year call.

Q. What is a trigger in a stress-testing plan?

A. A pre-agreed measurable level at which a named person must take a named action, written in calm times so the decision is not improvised in a crisis.

Q. What is a clawback in a waterfall?

A. An obligation on the sponsor to repay promote it received earlier if, at the end, investors have not received their capital and preferred return.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Kema here. Post-mortem weeks are where the phase's lessons stop being separate. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Describe a leverage spiral in four steps.

Answer: Value falls; a loan-to-value or coverage covenant is breached; cash is trapped or swept, so leasing and maintenance are starved; income and value fall again. Because equity is the first loss, a 15 percent fall in value on a 70 percent leveraged portfolio halves the equity.

Question 2. Why is a maturity wall dangerous even with good buildings?

Answer: Because it depends on the market on a fixed date, not on the buildings. Good buildings protect the recovery; they do not open a closed credit market.

Question 3. What was the root cause at General Growth Properties?

Answer: A mismatch between the life of the assets and the life of the debt, concentrated in time. Short-dated debt could not be refinanced when the market closed in 2008, and the company filed in April 2009.

Question 4. What is the difference between cross-default and cross-acceleration?

Answer: Cross-default treats another debt's default as a default here, even if that lender has done nothing. Cross-acceleration applies only once the other debt has actually been accelerated. Borrowers seek cross-acceleration with a threshold.

Question 5. Why does a guarantee come into play before value falls through the whole equity cushion?

Answer: Because default interest, receiver and sale costs are added to the lender's claim and deducted from proceeds, and starved income lowers value. In this week's example, half the demand was the cost of default itself.

Question 6. What do you bring to the meeting after a demand letter?

Answer: Your lawyer, a sworn liquidity statement, counsel's analysis of the claim, an agreed proposal and walk-away number, and the discipline to stay silent after proposing.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Ford named the three mechanisms: spirals, walls and guarantee calls. Ford and Roman took General Growth Properties through seven steps, giving Rule 46. Roman priced guarantees as expected loss and then as a correlated combined call. LEX read the chain from default to acceleration, cross-default and the guarantee itself. Roman reverse engineered a 6,000,000 dollar demand. Roman ran the meeting after the letter.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical debt summary from a developer's quarterly report and find the defects.

Debt summary. Total debt 60,000,000 dollars across three projects. All three loans mature in the second quarter of next year; we expect to refinance at current terms. Loan to value is 68 percent on average, inside the 75 percent covenants. Each project sits in its own special purpose vehicle, so a problem on one cannot affect the others. The sponsor's guarantees total 15,000,000 dollars; expected loss is about 1,500,000 dollars, comfortably covered by sponsor liquidity of 4,000,000 dollars.

The defects. First, all three loans mature in one quarter: a maturity wall, with no plan if the market is closed. Second, "refinance at current terms" is an assumption, not a plan; no stressed proceeds are shown. Third, an average loan to value hides the weakest project, which may already be near its covenant. Fourth, the claim that the vehicles are isolated ignores the guarantees and any cross-default to the sponsor; the sponsor connects all three. Fifth, the guarantee test uses expected loss, the average, rather than the combined call in a severe year, 15,000,000 dollars against 4,000,000 dollars of liquidity. Sixth, no caps, burn-offs or triggers are mentioned.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "How could this company fail with good buildings?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "In three ways, all driven by debt rather than by the buildings. A leverage spiral: values fall, a covenant breaks, cash is swept, maintenance and leasing suffer, and values fall again. A maturity wall: too many loans due together, so a closed credit market forces sales at the bottom. And guarantee calls: the sponsor's guarantees and cross-defaults connect projects that look separate, so one failure can reach all. General Growth Properties in 2009 showed the wall at scale: good malls, short debt, a closed market. Our controls are to ladder maturities so no year can force a sale, hold a reserve or unencumbered asset equal to the largest maturity, keep our own leverage ceiling inside the covenants, negotiate cross-acceleration, caps and burn-offs, and size liquidity to the combined call on all guarantees in one bad year. And if trouble comes, we act before default, because default itself is expensive."

Score yourself. Did you name all three mechanisms? Did you give one control for each? Did you finish in two minutes?

A practice habit for the week ahead

Draw your own debt map, even if it is hypothetical: every loan, its maturity, its covenant levels, every guarantee with cap and burn-off, and an arrow for every cross-default. Then write three numbers under it: the cash needed if no lender refinanced anything for twelve months, the combined guarantee call in one bad year, and your liquidity. If either of the first two exceeds the third, write the one action that would close the gap and the date you will take it.

Where you will meet this again

These mechanisms return in Week 75, when the post-mortem turns to partnerships and related-party dealing, and in Week 96, when it turns to personal wealth: concentration and guarantees on the personal balance sheet are the same spiral at the scale of a family. Learn the shape here and you will recognise it there.

Score yourself

Give yourself one point for each question answered aloud without looking, and one more for each answer that included a number. Ten or more is strong. Below eight, reread Day 3 and Day 5, where the arithmetic lives, and run the backward calculation on a building of your own before next week's checkpoint.

Then record the two-minute answer once more, aloud, and listen for whether you named the shared cause before the three mechanisms. That order is what makes the answer sound like judgment rather than a list.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is reading your loans one at a time. The control is the one-page map of every loan, maturity, guarantee and cross-default, reviewed quarterly.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the special purpose vehicle as a wall that guarantees cannot climb. Your signature is the ladder.

Callback

In Week 42, Priya taught the ring-fence of project finance. This week showed its limits: a ring-fence protects the project from its owner, but a guarantee runs straight through it, and, as one 2009 bankruptcy showed, even a structure built to stay out of a parent's insolvency depends on law and facts at the time.

Recap

Spirals, walls and guarantee calls share one cause, a falling market, so test them together. Ladder maturities, hold a reserve, set your own ceiling, read the cross-default chain, size to the combined call and act before default. Rule 46 holds it together.

head: The six questions
speak: This week came down to one sentence: debt kills through spirals, walls and guarantee calls, and all three share one cause. A leverage spiral turns falling value into falling cash through covenants and sweeps. A maturity wall asks for too much money on one date, and good buildings do not open a closed market; General Growth Properties showed that in 2009. Guarantee calls and cross-defaults connect projects that look separate, and they are called together, so I size my liquidity to the combined call in one bad year, not the average. Default interest and enforcement costs bring guarantees into play early, so I act before default. My controls: ladder maturities, hold a reserve or clean asset equal to the largest maturity, set my own leverage ceiling inside the covenants, negotiate cross-acceleration with caps and burn-offs, and keep one page that maps every loan, guarantee and link. Rule 46.
terms: Debt map — a one-page picture of every loan, maturity, guarantee and cross-default and how they connect.
Combined call — the total that could be demanded under all guarantees in a single severe year.
Unencumbered asset — a property or holding with no mortgage or charge on it, available to raise cash or offer as security.

hostile.q: Your three projects are in separate vehicles. Why should I worry about all three if one fails?
hostile.a: Because I connect them. My guarantees total 15,000,000 dollars and some loans cross-default to me, so a call on one could reach the others. That is why the maturities are now spread over three years, the cross-default clauses are being narrowed to cross-acceleration with a threshold, and my liquidity is sized to the combined call, not to the expected loss.
